food.text: Farming began in South America between 11,000 and 7,600 years ago, according to archaeobotanical evidence. The earliest crops were lerén (Goeppertia allouia) and arrowroot. Over time, people cultivated a more diverse array of plants.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: In the Amazon Basin, the slow shift from small foraging and hunter-gatherer groups to more advanced farming societies began over 10,000 years ago. The exact timing varied by sub-region. The systems that followed combined arboriculture with staple root and seed crops, and they supported stable settlements.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: By about 11,000 years ago, people in the tropical forest were staying longer at fixed locations and returning often to particular places. They shaped their surroundings by creating clearings in the forest and burning it. This was an early step toward managing the landscape for food.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: Early plant domestication in South America is thought to have been slow and gradual. About 6,000 years ago, the move from foraging and small-scale farming to larger, more sophisticated farming sped things up. Domestication then became rapid and diverse, making the Amazon a major source of domesticated plant species.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

food.text: Brazilian archaeologists often divide the deep past by geological epochs rather than by the traditional Stone Age labels. In this scheme, the Pleistocene was a time of hunters and gatherers at least 12,000 years ago. The Early Archaic then ran from 12,000 to 9,000 years ago.

Some 6,000 years ago, farming in the Amazon shifted to a larger scale and plant domestication sped up. By the time Europeans arrived, at least 83 plant species had been influenced by domestication. They included cacao, hot peppers, manioc, pineapple and sweet potato.
food.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

art.text: In the Baixão da Perna 1 cave, in the archeological area of São Raimundo Nonato, cave paintings dating back 10,500 years have been found. The cave paintings of this region have long fascinated experts.
At the site of Boqueirão da Pedra Furada, archaeologists found numerous cave paintings made in red pigment. The authors identify the painting tradition of this area as the "northeast tradition".

The earliest pottery ever found in the Western Hemisphere was excavated in the Amazon basin of Brazil. It was radiocarbon dated to over 8,000 years ago (6000 BC). Found near Santarém, it suggests the region supported a complex prehistoric culture.

The most abundant figures in the northeast tradition's cave paintings represent human beings, plants and animals, though purely abstract graphisms are also found. Some cave walls depict hunting scenes and ritual celebrations.
Besides the main northeast tradition, researchers have identified subtraditions of rock painting. Várzea Grande is found in the southeast of Piauí, and Seridó in Rio Grande do Norte.

According to some archaeologists, the themes of violence in ancient rock art would be linked to the technical development achieved in subsequent years. That development was responsible for promoting more efficient hunting strategies.

The northeastern painting tradition, which produced the red cave paintings of sites such as Boqueirão da Pedra Furada, concluded about 5,000 years ago. Its art therefore spanned thousands of years, beginning with paintings dated to 10,500 years ago.

science.text: Archaeo-botanical evidence indicates that food cultivation began in South America between 11,000 and 7,600 years ago. The earliest crops were lerén (Goeppertia allouia) and arrowroot. Plant domestication is thought to have been a slow and gradual process.
science.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

science.text: About 6,000 years ago, the shift from foraging and small-scale farming to larger and more sophisticated farming accelerated plant domestication in the Amazon. It became rapid and diverse, making the Amazon a major source of domesticated plants. Before European contact, at least 83 species had been influenced, including cacao, manioc and pineapple.
science.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

science.text: By about 11,000 years ago, evidence points to people staying longer at fixed locations within the tropical forest. They settled into their landscapes and frequently altered their environments by creating clearings in the forest or burning it.
science.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

science.text: The slow transition from small foraging and hunter-gatherer groups to more advanced agricultural societies began over 10,000 years ago in the Amazon Basin. The exact timing varied by sub-region. It later evolved into farming systems with arboriculture and staple root and seed crops.
science.source_title: Pre-Columbian agriculture in the Amazon Basin

science.text: In southern Brazil, the Uruguay phase of stone toolmaking dates from 11,555 to 8,640 BP. Its people made scrapers, bifacial blades and projectile points. It followed the Ibicuí tradition, whose simple artifacts were found in the Uruguay Basin.
In Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, archaeologists have located knives, scrapers and arrowheads dating from 8,500 to 6,500 years ago. These artifacts are known as the Vinitu tradition.

The Humaitá tradition, dated between 6,500 and 2,000 years ago, extends from São Paulo to Rio Grande do Sul. Its people made scrapers and awls, and also zooliths, which are stone statues in the shape of animals.

culture.text: In the Baixão da Perna 1 cave, in the São Raimundo Nonato archaeological area, cave paintings dating back 10,500 years have been found. The most abundant figures represent human beings, plants and animals, though purely abstract graphisms also appear.
Monte Alegre culture rock paintings were created at Caverna da Pedra Pintada in the Amazon, dating back to 9250–8550 BCE. They are counted among the lithic age art of South America.

The tembetá is a metal or stone rod placed in a lower lip piercing, used since the Neolithic period for body modification, spiritual protection and to indicate sexual maturity. According to the first studies of Jorge Fernández, tembetás originated in Planalto, Brazil.

Some cave walls in northeastern Brazil depict hunting scenes and ritual celebrations. The authors call the painting tradition of the area the "northeast tradition", and it concluded about 5,000 years ago.

Sites in the Santarém region of Brazil contain ceramic sherds dating between 5000 and 3000 BCE, among the earliest evidence of decorated pottery in South America. The ceramics were decorated with curvilinear incisions.

At the Boqueirão da Pedra Furada site, numerous cave paintings in red pigment were found. Researchers have also identified subtraditions of the northeast tradition, such as Várzea Grande in the southeast of Piauí and Seridó in Rio Grande do Norte.
The Santarém pottery overturned the assumption that the tropical forest was too poor in resources to support a complex prehistoric culture. It was radiocarbon-dated to 8,000 years old.

In tembetá initiation ceremonies, men and candidates drank chicha, a fermented maize beverage, to dull the pain while a specialist pierced the lip with a thick wooden needle. The tembetá was worn for the rest of the person's life and signified entry into adult life.

According to some archaeologists, the themes of violence in ancient rock art of northeastern Brazil may be linked to the technical development achieved in later years. That development, they suggest, promoted more efficient hunting strategies.

Many neolithic tribes of the Amazon demonstrated a deep scorn for peoples that did not use the tembetá. It offered protection against the negative action of the "owners of nature" and was the ritual adornment of the "souls that travel towards the land of beyond".
